People always ask me if my job is like television, and the honest answer is no. On television, a cross-examination is a duel. The lawyer shouts, the witness breaks down, and somebody confesses before the commercial break. In twenty years as a trial lawyer, I have never seen a confession in a courtroom. A good cross-examination is boring on purpose. I follow one rule: never ask a question you do not already know the answer to. Every question is a short step, and the witness can only say yes. And the work does not happen in the courtroom. Most of it happens months before, in depositions, in a conference room with no judge and no jury, where you find out what the witness is going to say. As for objections, I object maybe twice in a whole day. A lawyer jumping up every minute would lose the jury and annoy the judge.

Before I wrote for television, I spent four years as a paralegal at a firm in Chicago. Most of that time I was reviewing documents, thousands of them, looking for one email that somebody should never have sent. When I joined my first writers' room, the producer told me something I have never forgotten: the real work is invisible, so we cannot film it. And he was right. Nobody wants to watch a man reading in a basement. So I change the timeline. I take six months of discovery and turn it into one scene. That is poetic license, and I am comfortable with it. What I refuse to change is the way lawyers talk to each other: the politeness, the pressure, the silences. The scene I am proudest of has no courtroom at all. It is a phone call about a settlement, four minutes long, and nobody raises their voice once.

First, the client's complaint is filed in court, and the other side has a few weeks to respond. Over the next year, both sides exchange thousands of documents, reviewed line by line by associates and paralegals. Then the depositions begin: witnesses answer questions under oath in a conference room, with no judge and no jury. Six months before the trial date, with the evidence on the table, the two sides sit down to negotiate. Finally, a week before the trial, the case settles, and the courtroom scene that television promised never happens.
